title: VSEPR Theory and Shapes of Simple Molecules
topicTitle: VSEPR theory and shapes of simple molecules (BeF2, BF3, CH4, CH3Cl, PCl5, SF6, H2O, NH3, CO2, H2S, PH3)
notes: **VSEPR principle:** Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory states that electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves to minimize repulsion. Both bonding pairs and lone pairs occupy space and repel each other. The geometry is determined by the total number of electron domains (steric number).
**VSEPR notation:** AXₘEₙ, where A = central atom, X = bonding pair (bonded atom), E = lone pair. The sum m + n = steric number (total electron domains).

**Linear (AX₂, steric number 2):** BeF₂ has 2 bonding domains, 0 lone pairs. Bond angle = 180°. Be uses sp hybridization. Each Be–F bond is a σ bond. Beryllium has only 4 valence e⁻ (electron-deficient), but the linear geometry minimizes repulsion between the two bonding pairs.
**Linear (AX₂E₃, steric number 5):** XeF₂ has 2 bonding domains and 3 lone pairs. The lone pairs occupy equatorial positions, giving a linear molecular geometry. Bond angle = 180°.

**Trigonal planar (AX₃, steric number 3):** BF₃ has 3 bonding domains, 0 lone pairs. Bond angle = 120°. B uses sp² hybridization. Boron has only 6 valence e⁻ (electron-deficient), making BF₃ a strong Lewis acid. The molecule is planar because sp² orbitals lie in one plane at 120°.

**Bent/angular (AX₂E₁, steric number 3):** O₃ (ozone) has 2 bonding domains and 1 lone pair on the central O. The ideal trigonal planar angle (120°) is compressed to ~117° by the lone pair. The molecule is bent.

**Bent/angular (AX₂E₂, steric number 4):** H₂O has 2 bonding domains and 2 lone pairs on O. The ideal tetrahedral angle (109.5°) is compressed to 104.5° by the two lone pairs. H₂S is bent with a bond angle of ~92° — the smaller angle is because S is larger and less electronegative, so lone pair repulsion is less pronounced.

**Tetrahedral (AX₄, steric number 4):** CH₄ has 4 bonding domains, 0 lone pairs. Bond angle = 109.5°. C uses sp³ hybridization. Four equivalent C–H σ bonds. The tetrahedron is the most symmetric arrangement for 4 domains, minimizing all repulsions equally.

**Tetrahedral (AX₄, steric number 4):** CH₃Cl (chloromethane) has 4 bonding domains, 0 lone pairs. Geometry is tetrahedral but not regular — the H–C–H angle is slightly smaller than Cl–C–H angle because Cl is larger and more electronegative than H, pushing the H atoms slightly together.

**Trigonal pyramidal (AX₃E₁, steric number 4):** NH₃ has 3 bonding domains and 1 lone pair on N. The ideal tetrahedral angle (109.5°) is compressed to 107° by the lone pair. N uses sp³ hybridization. The molecule is pyramidal (not planar) because the lone pair occupies one vertex of a tetrahedron.

**Trigonal pyramidal (AX₃E₁, steric number 4):** PH₃ has a bond angle of ~93°, much smaller than NH₃ (107°). This is because P is larger and less electronegative than N, so the bonding pairs are farther from the nucleus and the lone pair exerts less additional compression. Some argue PH₃ uses nearly pure p orbitals (no hybridization) for bonding.

**Trigonal bipyramidal (AX₅, steric number 5):** PCl₅ has 5 bonding domains, 0 lone pairs. Uses sp³d hybridization. Three equatorial bonds at 120° to each other, two axial bonds at 90° to the equatorial plane. Axial bonds are longer and weaker than equatorial bonds because they experience more repulsion (3 × 90° interactions vs. 2 × 90° + 2 × 120°).

**Octahedral (AX₆, steric number 6):** SF₆ has 6 bonding domains, 0 lone pairs. Uses sp³d² hybridization. All S–F bonds are equivalent. Bond angles = 90°. Sulfur has 12 valence e⁻ (expanded octet). SF₆ is an extremely stable, inert gas used as electrical insulator.

**Square planar (AX₄E₂, steric number 6):** XeF₄ has 4 bonding domains and 2 lone pairs. The lone pairs occupy opposite (axial) positions to minimize repulsion. The 4 F atoms lie in a square plane. Bond angles = 90°. Xe has 8 bonding e⁻ + 4 non-bonding e⁻ = 12 total.

**Repulsion strength order:** lone pair–lone pair (lp–lp) > lone pair–bonding pair (lp–bp) > bonding pair–bonding pair (bp–bp). This explains why bond angles are compressed from ideal values when lone pairs are present. In H₂O (2 lp), the compression is greater than in NH₃ (1 lp).

**Effect of electronegativity on bond angles:** higher electronegativity of the surrounding atoms draws bonding pairs away from the central atom, reducing bp–bp repulsion and allowing lone pairs to compress the angle more. NH₃ (107°) > PH₃ (93°) > AsH₃ (92°) > SbH₃ (91°) — as the central atom gets larger, the bond angles decrease toward 90°.

**Real-world relevance — water's bent shape:** the bent geometry of H₂O (104.5°) combined with its polar O–H bonds makes water a polar molecule with a large dipole moment (1.85 D). This is responsible for water's unique properties: high boiling point (H-bonding), solvent capability, and density anomaly (ice floats).

**Real-world relevance — ammonia's pyramidal shape:** the pyramidal geometry of NH₃ (107°) makes it a polar molecule (μ = 1.47 D). The lone pair on nitrogen gives NH₃ its characteristic Lewis basicity, enabling it to form coordinate bonds with metal ions (e.g., [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ deep blue complex).

**Real-world relevance — CO₂ linear geometry:** CO₂ is linear (180°) so the two C=O bond dipoles cancel exactly, making CO₂ nonpolar. This is crucial for its role as a greenhouse gas — its vibrational modes (bending at 667 cm⁻¹) create a temporary dipole that absorbs infrared radiation.

**Real-world relevance — PCl₅ in solution:** PCl₅ is trigonal bipyramidal in the gas and solid phases. In solution, it ionizes: PCl₅ → PCl₄⁺ (tetrahedral) + PCl₆⁻ (octahedral). This demonstrates that VSEPR shapes can change with the chemical environment.

**Real-world relevance — SF₆ as insulator:** SF₆'s octahedral geometry (AX₆, no lone pairs) makes it nonpolar and extremely stable. Its high electron affinity and large size make it an excellent electronegative gas for high-voltage circuit breakers. It is ~100× more effective than air as an insulator.

**Limitations of VSEPR:** VSEPR is a qualitative model that works well for simple main-group compounds but fails for transition metal complexes, molecules with d-orbital participation, and some hypervalent species. Advanced treatments use molecular orbital theory.

**VSEPR vs. hybridization:** VSEPR predicts geometry from electron repulsion; hybridization explains bonding using orbital mixing. Both predict the same shapes for simple molecules, but VSEPR is more fundamental (based on observed repulsions) while hybridization is a mathematical convenience.
confusion: PCl₅ has all 5 P–Cl bonds equal in length — False. In PCl₅ (trigonal bipyramidal), axial bonds are longer (~219 pm) than equatorial bonds (~204 pm) because axial bonds experience 3 repulsive interactions at 90° (with equatorial bonds) while equatorial bonds experience only 2 (with axial bonds). This is a direct consequence of VSEPR geometry.

H₂O and CO₂ have the same number of electron domains around the central atom — False. H₂O has 4 electron domains (2 bonding + 2 lone pairs, steric number 4, tetrahedral electron geometry, bent molecular geometry). CO₂ has 2 electron domains (2 double bonds, steric number 2, linear). Double bonds count as one domain in VSEPR.

NH₃ and PH₃ have similar bond angles because they are in the same group — False. NH₃ has a bond angle of 107°, while PH₃ has ~93°. The large difference is because N is smaller and more electronegative, keeping bonding pairs closer to the nucleus where lone pair repulsion is more effective. P's larger size means bonding pairs are farther away and lone pair effect is weaker.

All AX₄ molecules are tetrahedral — False. AX₄E₂ molecules (like XeF₄) have steric number 6 and are square planar, not tetrahedral. The presence of lone pairs changes the geometry. Only AX₄ with steric number 4 (no lone pairs) is tetrahedral.

Bond angles always decrease with lone pairs — Not always. In PCl₅, the axial-equatorial angle is 90° (compressed from ideal). But in some cases, lone pairs can actually INCREASE certain angles by pushing bonding pairs together. The effect depends on the specific geometry and the number/position of lone pairs.

VSEPR works equally well for all elements — False. VSEPR works best for main-group elements (Groups 1, 2, 13–18). It often fails for transition metal complexes (where d-orbital effects dominate), heavy elements (where inert pair effect matters), and molecules with significant covalent character. For example, VSEPR poorly predicts the geometry of some ClF₃ derivatives.
practice: Problem: Predict the shape and bond angles of ClF₃ using VSEPR. Solution: Cl has 7 valence e⁻, 3 F atoms contribute 3 e⁻, total = 10 e⁻ = 5 domains. 3 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs = steric number 5. Geometry: trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry. The 2 lone pairs occupy equatorial positions (to minimize lp–lp repulsion). Molecular geometry: T-shaped. Bond angles: F–Cl–F ≈ 87.5° (slightly less than 90° due to lone pair compression).

Problem: Compare the bond angles of H₂O (104.5°), NH₃ (107°), and CH₄ (109.5°) using VSEPR. Solution: All have steric number 4 (tetrahedral electron geometry). CH₄ has 0 lone pairs → ideal 109.5°. NH₃ has 1 lone pair → lp–bp repulsion compresses angle to 107°. H₂O has 2 lone pairs → stronger lp–lp repulsion compresses angle further to 104.5°. The trend: more lone pairs → smaller bond angle.

Problem: Explain why the bond angle in H₂S (92°) is smaller than in H₂O (104.5°) despite both being AX₂E₂. Solution: S is larger and less electronegative than O. In H₂S, the bonding pairs are farther from the nucleus, so bp–bp repulsion is weaker. Additionally, S may use nearly pure p orbitals (no hybridization) for bonding, giving angles close to 90°. In H₂O, O's smaller size and higher electronegativity favor sp³ hybridization with significant lone pair compression.

Problem: Draw the Lewis structure of XeF₄ and predict its geometry using VSEPR. Solution: Xe has 8 valence e⁻, 4 F contribute 4 e⁻, total = 12 e⁻ = 6 domains. 4 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs. Steric number 6 → octahedral electron geometry. The 2 lone pairs occupy opposite (axial) positions to minimize repulsion. Molecular geometry: square planar. Bond angles: 90°. XeF₄ is nonpolar because the 4 Xe–F dipoles cancel in the plane.

Problem: Using VSEPR, predict the shape of I₃⁻ (triiodide ion) and explain why it is linear. Solution: Central I has 7 valence e⁻, each terminal I contributes 1 e⁻, +1 charge = 10 e⁻ = 5 domains. 2 bonding pairs + 3 lone pairs. Steric number 5 → trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry. The 3 lone pairs occupy equatorial positions (maximizing separation). Molecular geometry: linear. Bond angle: 180°. The central I has 3 lone pairs and 2 bonds, giving it an expanded octet (10 e⁻).

Problem: Compare the geometries of SF₄ and XeF₄ using VSEPR theory. Solution: SF₄: S has 6 valence e⁻ + 4 F = 10 e⁻ = 5 domains. 4 bonding + 1 lone pair. See-saw geometry (distorted tetrahedron). Bond angles: axial-equatorial ~90°, equatorial-equatorial ~120°. XeF₄: Xe has 8 valence e⁻ + 4 F = 12 e⁻ = 6 domains. 4 bonding + 2 lone pairs. Square planar geometry. Bond angles: 90°. The extra lone pair in XeF₄ vs. SF₄ changes the geometry from see-saw to square planar.
universalFacts: VSEPR theory was developed by Ronald Gillespie and Ronald Nyholm in the 1950s, building on earlier work by Nevil Sidgwick and Herbert Powell. It remains the simplest and most widely taught method for predicting molecular geometry.

The bond angle compression by lone pairs follows the order: lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp. This explains why H₂O (104.5°) has a smaller angle than NH₃ (107°) despite both having tetrahedral electron geometry.
In trigonal bipyramidal geometry, lone pairs always occupy equatorial positions because equatorial sites have more space (120° angles) compared to axial sites (90° angles), minimizing repulsion.
Double and triple bonds count as a single electron domain in VSEPR theory, but they occupy slightly more space than single bonds, causing small distortions in bond angles.
The VSEPR model is purely qualitative — it predicts shapes but cannot calculate exact bond angles. Computational quantum chemistry (e.g., DFT) is needed for quantitative predictions.
